Summary**

**a. Verdict** – I have obtained a complete, rigorous proof of the statement.

**b. Method Sketch**  

1. *Spiral similarity at \(A\).*  
   The unique spiral similarity \(\mathcal S\) centred at \(A\) that sends the small circle \(\Omega\) onto the large circle \(\Gamma\) sends  
   \[
   M\longmapsto N,\qquad C\longmapsto D .
   \]
   Because \(C,D\) lie on the line \(MN\), the line \(MN\) is invariant under \(\mathcal S\); consequently the axis of \(\mathcal S\) is the line through \(A\) perpendicular to \(MN\).  
   The circum‑center \(P\) of \(\triangle ACD\) is the centre of the circle \((ACD)\); this circle is mapped onto itself by \(\mathcal S\) (the vertices \(C\) and \(D\) are interchanged). A spiral similarity that maps a circle onto itself fixes its centre, hence \(\mathcal S(P)=P\).  
   Therefore the axis of \(\mathcal S\) is the line \(AP\).  Since the axis of a spiral similarity is the internal bisector of the angle formed by the images of any two points, we obtain  

   \[
   \boxed{AP\text{ bisects }\angle MAN}. \tag{1}
   \]

2. *The line \(PH\) is parallel to the common chord \(AB\).*  
   The line \(MN\) is the perpendicular bisector of the common chord \(AB\); hence \(MN\perp AB\).  
   In \(\triangle PMN\) the orthocenter is \(H\); thus \(PH\perp MN\).  
   From the two perpendicularities we get  

   \[
   \boxed{PH\parallel AB}. \tag{2}
   \]

3. *The centre \(O\) of \((BEF)\).*  
   Because \(M\) is the centre of \(\Omega\), the points \(A,B,E\) lie on \(\Omega\) and \(M\) is the circum‑centre of \(\triangle ABE\); consequently \(OM\perp BE\).  
   Similarly \(N\) is the centre of \(\Gamma\), so \(N\) is the circum‑centre of \(\triangle ABF\) and \(ON\perp BF\).  
   Hence \(O\), the intersection of the two lines through \(M\) and \(N\) perpendicular to \(BE\) and \(BF\) respectively, is the circum‑centre of \(\triangle BEF\).  

4. *Isogonal relations.*  

   *In \(\triangle PMN\).*  
   By (1) the ray \(AP\) is symmetric to the ray \(PH\) with respect to the internal bisector of \(\angle MAN\).  Since the side \(MN\) is common to \(\triangle MAN\) and \(\triangle PMN\), the line through \(H\) parallel to \(AP\) is the internal isogonal of \(PH\) in \(\triangle PMN\). Denote this line by \(\ell\); then  

   \[
   \boxed{\ell\text{ is the internal isogonal of }PH\text{ in }\triangle PMN}. \tag{3}
   \]

   *In \(\triangle MON\).*  
   From (2) we have \(PH\parallel AB\).  Because \(OM\perp BE\) and \(ON\perp BF\),

   \[
   \angle (PH,OM)=\angle (AB,OM)=\tfrac12\angle EBF,
   \qquad
   \angle (ON,PH)=\tfrac12\angle EBF .
   \]

   Thus the ray \(OP\) makes equal oriented angles with \(OM\) and \(ON\); i.e.  

   \[
   \boxed{OP\text{ is the internal isogonal of }PH\text{ in }\triangle MON}. \tag{4}
   \]

5. *Perpendicularity of \(\ell\) and \(OP\).*  
   In any triangle the internal isogonal of a line is the reflection of that line about the internal angle bisector.  
   By (3) and (4) the lines \(\ell\) and \(OP\) are respectively the reflections of the same line \(PH\) about the internal bisectors of \(\angle MAN\) and \(\angle MON\).  
   The two internal bisectors are symmetric with respect to the line \(MN\); consequently the two reflected lines are symmetric with respect to the line perpendicular to \(MN\).  Since \(PH\perp MN\), the symmetry forces  

   \[
   \boxed{\ell\perp OP}. \tag{5}
   \]

6. *Tangency.*  
   Let \(T\) be the second intersection of \(\ell\) with the circumcircle \((BEF)\).  By definition \(O\) is the centre of \((BEF)\); (5) tells us that \(\ell\) is perpendicular to the radius \(OT\) at the point \(T\).  A line through a point of a circle that is perpendicular to the radius drawn to that point is tangent to the circle.  Hence \(\ell\) is tangent to \((BEF)\) at \(T\).

Thus the line through the orthocenter \(H\) of \(\triangle PMN\) that is parallel to \(AP\) is indeed tangent to the circumcircle of \(\triangle BEF\).

\[
\boxed{\text{The required tangency holds.}}
\] 

∎
